props.title: Four Weddings and a Funeral

sections.content: Four Weddings and a Funeral (1994) revolutionized British romantic comedies with its perfect blend of Hugh Grant's stammering charm and Richard Curtis's razor-sharp writing. The film's structure - following a group of friends through five major ceremonies - created a template that countless rom-coms tried to replicate. Its success ($245.7 million worldwide on a £3 million budget) kicked off the 1990s British rom-com renaissance, leading directly to Notting Hill (1999) and Love Actually (2003). Grant's Charles became the definitive bumbling-but-lovable British leading man, while Andie MacDowell's Carrie brought American glamour to the very British proceedings.

sections.content: The film's genius lies in how it balances comedy and tragedy. The "funeral" portion, featuring John Hannah's heart-wrenching reading of W.H. Auden's "Funeral Blues," proved that romantic comedies could handle profound grief without losing their charm. This emotional depth influenced later films like About Time (2013) and Death at a Funeral (2007), showing how comedy and mortality could coexist meaningfully.

Richard Curtis's screenplay masterfully juggles its ensemble cast, giving each character memorable moments while maintaining Charles and Carrie's central romance. This approach influenced countless films, from My Best Friend's Wedding (1997) to Bridget Jones's Diary (2001), establishing the importance of strong supporting characters in romantic comedies. The film's success also helped launch Working Title Films as a major force in British cinema. SUBHEAD: Impact on British Cinema and Rom-Com Genre

sections.content: The film's success created a distinct "British rom-com" style characterized by self-deprecating humor, rain-soaked London streets, and complicated love affairs among the middle-class. This influenced everything from The Full Monty (1997) to About a Boy (2002). The film's ability to export British humor internationally paved the way for later successes like Shaun of the Dead (2004) and Hot Fuzz (2007), proving British comedy could travel.
